claims.text: The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy meets current density and room-temperature performance specifications.
Yttrium is a lightweight reactive element suitable for minor addition to the alloy.
Adding approximately 0.5 at% yttrium during melting and then thermally exposing the alloy in a low-oxygen atmosphere will promote in situ Y2O3 formation.
The intervention will produce uniformly distributed nanoscale Y2O3 particles in the alloy matrix.
Fine Y2O3 nanoprecipitates impede dislocation motion at high temperature.
Fine Y2O3 nanoprecipitates impede grain-boundary sliding at high temperature.
Impeded dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding will increase high-temperature creep resistance.
Dispersion strengthening by Y2O3 will increase high-temperature yield strength.
The low yttrium concentration and fine oxide dispersion will have minimal effect on overall alloy density.
The low yttrium concentration and fine oxide dispersion will preserve room-temperature ductility or toughness.
The modified alloy will have greater high-temperature yield strength than the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy will have greater creep resistance than the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy will retain room-temperature performance comparable to that of the unmodified alloy.
The magnitude of the high-temperature improvement depends on Y2O3 particle size, distribution, and volume fraction.

contradictions.description: The headline hypothesis says density will not increase, whereas the mechanism and boundary permit a minimal or statistically insignificant density increase.
